items.readable_text:
Content:
In previous lessons, we explored converting larger units of mass to smaller ones. In this lesson, we will learn how to convert smaller units of mass to larger ones.

Content:
To convert between customary units of mass, we use the following unit conversions:

Content:
- [MATH: 1] ton [MATH: = 2,000] pounds
- [MATH: 1] pound [MATH: =16] ounces

Content:
We can think of unit conversions of mass concretely by picturing a set of weighing scales.

Content:
For example, if we placed a [MATH: 1\,\textrm{lb}] mass on one scale and sixteen [MATH: 1\,\textrm{oz}] masses on the other, the scales would balance perfectly.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/a370f6b12699c3eaa0b945e6fa628d17]

Content:
Similarly, we can picture a set of weighing scales showing the equivalence between [MATH: 1] ton and [MATH: 2,000\,\textrm{lb}.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/f4f953a8b7013f4583684c23a5d75c3d]

Content:
Let's get some practice at converting between customary units of mass.

Content:
For example, suppose we want to convert [MATH: 320] ounces to pounds. We start with the unit conversion between pounds and ounces:

Content:
[MATH: 1\, \textrm{pound} =16\, \textrm{ounces}]

Content:
Since we are converting from ounces to pounds, we divide both sides of the above equation by [MATH: 16] and obtain the following:

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{1}{16} \, \textrm{pounds} = 1 \, \textrm{ounce}]

Content:
The right-hand side reads [MATH: 1\,\textrm{ounce},] and we want to know how many pounds are in [MATH: \color{blue}320] ounces. So, we multiply both sides of this equation by [MATH: {\color{blue}{320}}.]

Content:
[MATH: 320 × (1)/(16)pounds|= 320 × 1ounce; (320)/(16)pounds|= 320ounces; (320 ÷ 4)/(16 ÷ 4)pounds|= 320ounces; (80)/(4)pounds|= 320ounces; 20pounds|= 320ounces]

Therefore, [MATH: 320] ounces equals [MATH: 20] pounds.

sections.normalized_html: What is [MATH: 132\,\textrm{oz}] in [MATH: \textrm{lb}?]
EXPLANATION

We need to convert [MATH: 132] ounces to pounds.

We start with the unit conversion between pounds and ounces:

[MATH: 1\, \textrm{lb} =16\, \textrm{oz}]

Now, we divide both sides by [MATH: 16] and obtain the following:

[MATH: \dfrac{1}{16} \, \textrm{lb} = 1 \, \textrm{oz}]

We want to figure out how many pounds are in [MATH: 132] ounces. So, we multiply both sides of the above equation by [MATH: 132{:}]

[MATH: 132 × (1)/(16)lb|= 132 × 1oz; (132)/(16)lb|= 132oz; (132 ÷ 2)/(16 ÷ 2)lb|= 132oz; (66)/(8)lb|= 132oz; 8(2)/(8)lb|= 132oz; 8(1)/(4)lb|= 132oz]

Therefore, [MATH: 132\,\textrm{oz}] equals [MATH: 8\,\dfrac{1}{4}\,\textrm{lb}.]

sections.normalized_html: How many tons are in [MATH: 1,600\,\textrm{lb}?]
EXPLANATION

We need to convert [MATH: 1,600] pounds to tons.

We start with the unit conversion between tons and pounds:

[MATH: 1\, \textrm{ton} =2,000\, \textrm{pounds}]

Now, we divide both sides by [MATH: 2,000] and obtain the following:

[MATH: \dfrac{1}{2,000} \, \textrm{tons} =1\, \textrm{pound}]

We want to figure out how many tons are in [MATH: 1,600] pounds. So, we multiply both sides of the above equation by [MATH: 1,600{:}]

[MATH: 1, 600 × (1)/(2, 000)tons|= 1, 600 × 1pound; (1, 600)/(2, 000)tons|= 1, 600pounds; (1, 600 ÷ 100)/(2, 000 ÷ 100)tons|= 1, 600pounds; (16)/(20)tons|= 1, 600pounds; (16 ÷ 4)/(20 ÷ 4)tons|= 1, 600pounds; (4)/(5)tons|= 1, 600pounds]

Therefore, [MATH: 1,600] pounds is equal to [MATH: \dfrac{4}{5}] tons.

sections.normalized_html: What is [MATH: 15,100\,\textrm{g}] measured in [MATH: \textrm{kg}?]
EXPLANATION

We need to convert [MATH: 15,100] grams to kilograms.

We start with the unit conversion between kilograms and grams:

[MATH: 1 \,\textrm{kg} = 1,000 \,\textrm{g}]

Now, we divide both sides by [MATH: 1,000] and obtain the following:

[MATH: \dfrac{1}{1,000} \,\textrm{kg} = 1 \,\textrm{g}]

We want to figure out how many kilograms are in [MATH: 15,100] grams. So, we multiply both sides of the above equation by [MATH: 15,100{:}]

[MATH: 15, 100 × (1)/(1, 000)kg|= 15, 100 × 1g; (15, 100 ÷ 1, 000)kg|= 15, 100g; 15.1kg|= 15, 100g]

Therefore, [MATH: 15,100 \, \textrm{g}] equals [MATH: 15.1 \, \textrm{kg}.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
In previous lessons, we explored converting larger units of mass to smaller ones. In this lesson, we will learn how to convert smaller units of mass to larger ones.

Content:
To convert between customary units of mass, we use the following unit conversions:

Content:
- [MATH: 1] ton [MATH: = 2,000] pounds
- [MATH: 1] pound [MATH: =16] ounces

Content:
We can think of unit conversions of mass concretely by picturing a set of weighing scales.

Content:
For example, if we placed a [MATH: 1\,\textrm{lb}] mass on one scale and sixteen [MATH: 1\,\textrm{oz}] masses on the other, the scales would balance perfectly.

Item 2 — Tutorial: A Worked Example

Content:
For example, suppose we want to convert [MATH: 320] ounces to pounds. We start with the unit conversion between pounds and ounces:

Content:
[MATH: 1\, \textrm{pound} =16\, \textrm{ounces}]

Content:
Since we are converting from ounces to pounds, we divide both sides of the above equation by [MATH: 16] and obtain the following:

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{1}{16} \, \textrm{pounds} = 1 \, \textrm{ounce}]

Content:
The right-hand side reads [MATH: 1\,\textrm{ounce},] and we want to know how many pounds are in [MATH: \color{blue}320] ounces. So, we multiply both sides of this equation by [MATH: {\color{blue}{320}}.]

Content:
[MATH: 320 × (1)/(16)pounds|= 320 × 1ounce; (320)/(16)pounds|= 320ounces; (320 ÷ 4)/(16 ÷ 4)pounds|= 320ounces; (80)/(4)pounds|= 320ounces; 20pounds|= 320ounces]

Content:
Therefore, [MATH: 320] ounces equals [MATH: 20] pounds.
